title: 13 — PySpark DataFrame Cookbook
html:
13 — PySpark DataFrame Cookbook

The one idea: almost every PySpark job is the same dozen moves: read, select, filter, add columns, join, aggregate, window, deduplicate, merge, write. Learn each with its SQL twin, and know which ones cause a shuffle.

1. What it is

A task-by-task reference for the PySpark DataFrame API, with the equivalent Spark SQL and a note on cost. The Apache Spark chapter explains what happens underneath: lazy evaluation, stages, shuffles and joins.

The code is not run in this note's build environment (PySpark needs a JVM and was not installed). It uses the public pyspark.sql API. Try it in a Databricks notebook (hands-on labs).

from pyspark.sql import functions as F, Window

2. Why it matters

Fluency here is the difference between writing a pipeline in an hour and writing it in a day, and between a job that shuffles once and one that shuffles ten times.

3. The recipes

3.1 Read and write

Task PySpark SQL
Read a table spark.table("fin.silver.nav") SELECT * FROM fin.silver.nav
Read files spark.read.format("csv").option("header", True).load(path) read_files(path, format => 'csv', header => true)
Write a table df.write.mode("append").saveAsTable("t") INSERT INTO t SELECT ...
Overwrite one partition safely df.write.mode("overwrite").option("replaceWhere", "nav_date = '2026-10-23'").saveAsTable("t") INSERT INTO t REPLACE WHERE nav_date = '2026-10-23' SELECT ...

3.2 Select, filter, derive (narrow: no shuffle)

df = (spark.table("fin.silver.nav")
        .select("isin", "nav_date", "nav")
        .where((F.col("nav") > 0) & F.col("isin").startswith("INF"))
        .withColumn("nav_x100", F.col("nav") * 100)
        .withColumn("month", F.date_trunc("MONTH", "nav_date"))
        .withColumn("band", F.when(F.col("nav") < 10, "low").when(F.col("nav") < 100, "mid").otherwise("high")))

3.3 Aggregate (wide: shuffle)

monthly = df.groupBy("isin", "month").agg(F.min("nav").alias("min_nav"), F.max("nav").alias("max_nav"),
                                          F.count("*").alias("days"), F.avg("nav").alias("avg_nav"))

3.4 Join

master = spark.table("fin.silver.fund_master")            # small table
enriched = df.join(F.broadcast(master), on="isin", how="left")   # broadcast: no shuffle of the big side
missing = df.join(master, on="isin", how="left_anti")     # NAV rows with no master record
Join type Returns
inner Matching rows only
left All left rows, with nulls where unmatched
left_anti Left rows with no match (great for "orphans")
left_semi Left rows with a match, left columns only

3.5 Window functions

w = Window.partitionBy("isin").orderBy("nav_date")
with_change = (df.withColumn("prev_nav", F.lag("nav").over(w))
                 .withColumn("pct_change", (F.col("nav") / F.col("prev_nav") - 1) * 100)
                 .withColumn("rolling_5d", F.avg("nav").over(w.rowsBetween(-4, 0))))

SQL twin: LAG(nav) OVER (PARTITION BY isin ORDER BY nav_date).

3.6 Deduplicate (keep the latest per key)

latest = (spark.table("fin.bronze.nav_raw")
            .withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(Window.partitionBy("isin", "nav_date").orderBy(F.desc("ingested_at"))))
            .where("rn = 1").drop("rn"))

dropDuplicates(["isin", "nav_date"]) keeps an arbitrary row, so use row_number when "latest" matters.

3.7 Merge (upsert)

from delta.tables import DeltaTable
target = DeltaTable.forName(spark, "fin.silver.fund_master")
(target.alias("t").merge(updates.alias("s"), "t.isin = s.isin")
   .whenMatchedUpdate(condition="t.row_hash <> s.row_hash", set={"name": "s.name", "row_hash": "s.row_hash"})
   .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
   .execute())

For append-only, bitemporal tables, insert new versions and close old ones instead of updating in place (storage module).

3.8 Semi-structured data

payload = spark.table("fin.bronze.vendor_json")
parsed = payload.select(F.from_json("body", "isin STRING, rating STRING, outlook STRING").alias("j")).select("j.*")
exploded = spark.table("fin.bronze.holdings").select("fund_id", F.explode("positions").alias("p")).select("fund_id", "p.*")

3.9 User-defined functions

  • Prefer built-in functions. They are optimised and run in Photon.
  • If you need Python logic, use a pandas UDF (vectorised) rather than a row-at-a-time UDF:
import pandas as pd
@F.pandas_udf("double")
def clean_pct(s: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    return pd.to_numeric(s.str.replace("%", "", regex=False), errors="coerce") / 100
df2 = spark.table("fin.bronze.factsheet_fields").withColumn("ter", clean_pct("ter_text"))

3.10 Inspect and debug

Need Call
See the plan df.explain("formatted")
Peek safely df.limit(20).display() (Databricks) or .show(20)
Schema df.printSchema()
Count per key, to spot skew df.groupBy("isin").count().orderBy(F.desc("count"))

4. Code

All code is in section 3, and not run in this note's build environment.

5. Common mistakes

  1. collect() on a big DataFrame. It pulls everything to the driver. Aggregate or limit first.
  2. Python UDFs for simple logic. Use built-in functions.
  3. Joining two big tables when one side could be filtered first. Filter early.
  4. dropDuplicates when you mean "latest". Use row_number.
  5. Many small appends. Batch them, and let maintenance compact.

6. Exercise (2 hours)

Rewrite the Silver step of the hands-on labs in PySpark: type the columns, deduplicate by latest ingestion, quarantine failures with a reason column, and add a 5-day rolling average. Compare explain() output before and after adding a broadcast join to a small master table.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. Which of select, groupBy, join and withColumn cause a shuffle?
  2. When is left_anti useful?
  3. Why prefer a pandas UDF to a plain Python UDF?
  4. What does replaceWhere protect against?
  5. Why is dropDuplicates not enough for "keep the latest"?

Answers

  1. groupBy, and join unless one side is broadcast. select and withColumn are narrow.
  2. Finding rows with no match on the other side, such as orphan records.
  3. It processes whole columns at a time through Arrow, which is far faster than row-by-row calls.
  4. Overwriting more data than intended. Only the matching slice is replaced.
  5. It keeps an arbitrary row per key, not a chosen one.
